buying-equipment|restaurants-and-hospita.h1: Finance for buying equipment in restaurants and hospitality
buying-equipment|restaurants-and-hospita.title: Equipment Finance for Restaurants and Hospitality | Loanleaf
buying-equipment|restaurants-and-hospita.desc: How UK restaurants, cafés, pubs and hotels finance kitchen and front-of-house equipment, and which loan types tend to suit. Free introduction to a broker.
buying-equipment|restaurants-and-hospita.lead: Ovens, coffee machines and cellar kit cost most when they fail mid-service, so finance should match the kit’s working life.
intro: A commercial kitchen is a collection of machines that each cost four or five figures and tend to fail at the worst moment. A combi oven, a walk-in cold room, a dishwasher, a coffee machine, a till system and a cellar cooling unit can add up to well over £100,000 for a new site, and a single failed fridge on a Friday can cost more in lost covers than the repair. Most operators prefer to keep cash for rent, wages and stock.

Asset finance, usually hire purchase, is the common route because the equipment is the security and the payments can be spread over three to seven years. Newer, higher-value items such as a full kitchen fit-out may suit a larger package, while a quick replacement of one machine may suit an unsecured loan. A broker will look at how long you have traded and how steady your takings are before suggesting a structure.
uses: Replacing a failed machine
A walk-in fridge or dishwasher breaks mid-season and needs replacing within days. Finance lets the business keep trading without spending the month’s cash buffer on one invoice.
Fitting out a second site
A new kitchen, bar and furniture are bought together and paid for over several years, so opening costs do not drain the working capital needed for the first quiet months.
Upgrading the coffee and drinks setup
A café buys a better espresso machine, grinders and a cold-brew system to lift drinks sales, and spreads the cost across the years the machine earns its keep.
Hotel and function equipment
Laundry machines, banqueting furniture, AV for events or a new spa area are financed as separate assets, each with a term that matches its useful life.
fit: Typical amounts and terms

A single machine might be £3,000 to £15,000 over two to five years, while a full kitchen fit-out can run into six figures over five to seven. Term length usually tracks how long the equipment is expected to work, so a dishwasher is financed over a shorter term than fixed catering infrastructure.
What lenders look at

Lenders check how long the venue has traded, the strength of card takings and bank statements, and whether rent and existing finance are being paid on time. For a new site they may ask for trading history from your existing venue and a plan for how the equipment will earn.
Structure and seasonality

Some agreements allow a lower first payment, a deposit or a seasonal payment profile that fits a hotel or seaside café with a quiet winter. Fixed monthly payments are simpler to budget against, but they continue in January whatever the covers are.
considerations: Fixtures and landlords

Equipment fixed into a leased unit can raise questions about who owns it if you leave. Check your lease and the finance agreement, as some lenders want the right to collect the asset from the premises.
Used and specialist kit
Second-hand ovens or bespoke cellar systems may be harder to finance because lenders worry about resale value. Expect a shorter term, a larger deposit or a request for a supplier valuation.
When it is not the right fit

If the real problem is a slow month rather than a purchase, a revolving facility or merchant cash advance may suit better than tying yourself to fixed payments for a machine. A broker can explain the alternatives.
faqs: Can I finance second-hand kitchen equipment?

Often yes, though lenders look more closely at age, condition and who is selling it. A dealer with a clear invoice and warranty is easier to finance than a private sale. Terms may be shorter and a deposit larger than for new kit, and a broker can tell you what lenders in this area are willing to consider.
Is hire purchase or leasing better for catering equipment?

Hire purchase suits equipment you plan to use for its whole life, such as ovens and cold rooms, because you usually own it at the end. Leasing can suit items that are replaced often, such as tills and coffee machines. Tax and VAT treatment differs, so check with your accountant before signing.
Does the equipment have to be new?

No. Lenders can finance used equipment, but they usually prefer newer items with an invoice from a recognised supplier. Age and condition affect the term offered. Some also want the asset to be identifiable, for example by serial number, so they can record it as security.
Can a new restaurant site get equipment finance?

It is possible if the company has been trading for at least six months and can show the existing venue or the wider business is performing. Lenders may ask for a business plan and management accounts for the new site, plus a deposit. A broker can advise how to present the application.
What happens if the machine breaks while I am still paying?

You usually remain responsible for the payments, because the agreement is separate from the supplier’s warranty. Check that warranty and maintenance cover run at least as long as the finance term, and consider insurance for breakdown. This is worth discussing with the broker and supplier before signing.

buying-vehicles|restaurants-and-hospital.h1: Finance for buying vehicles in restaurants and hospitality
buying-vehicles|restaurants-and-hospital.title: Vehicle Finance for Restaurants and Hospitality | Loanleaf
buying-vehicles|restaurants-and-hospital.desc: How UK restaurants, caterers, pubs and hotels finance delivery vans, refrigerated vehicles and minibuses, and which loan types tend to suit. Free introduction.
buying-vehicles|restaurants-and-hospital.lead: Delivery vans, refrigerated vehicles and guest transport are financed over a term that matches the miles they will do, not the menu.
intro: Most restaurants do not own vehicles, but several hospitality businesses depend on them. A catering company needs refrigerated vans on the road before every event, a hotel may run a minibus to the station, a brewery or pub group delivers kegs, and a growing café with a delivery arm needs a small fleet for local orders. These vehicles work hard, collect mileage quickly and lose value fast, so tying up cash in them can be hard to justify.

Asset finance is the usual route, with the vehicle acting as security. Hire purchase leaves the business owning the vehicle at the end, while contract hire suits operators who prefer to hand back and replace every few years. A broker will ask how the vehicle earns, whether that is event income, delivery revenue or guest transfers, because lenders want to see the payment covered by the work the vehicle does.
uses: Refrigerated vans for catering
A caterer buys a chilled van with temperature logging so food reaches weddings and corporate events safely, with the payments planned around the busy summer and Christmas periods.
Delivery fleet for a café or restaurant group
Several small vans or electric cargo bikes are financed together to serve a delivery area, with each vehicle’s cost tied to the orders it carries.
Hotel and guest transport
A minibus or people carrier is leased for airport and station transfers, with a term matching how long the hotel expects to run the service.
Pub and brewery drays
A pub group or small brewery finances a dray lorry or van for deliveries to venues, a larger purchase that often runs over five years or more.
fit: Typical amounts and terms

A panel van might be £15,000 to £35,000 over three to five years, while a refrigerated van or small lorry can be £40,000 to £90,000. Lenders usually set the term against the vehicle’s expected life and mileage, and a deposit of 10% or more is common.
What lenders look at

They check that the vehicle will be used for business, the company’s trading record, and whether existing finance is up to date. Because the vehicle is security, lenders also look at its make, age and value, so mainstream models are generally easier to finance than specialist conversions.
Own or hand back

Hire purchase gives ownership and no mileage limit, which suits a van used heavily every day. Contract hire gives a lower monthly outlay and removes resale risk, but mileage and condition limits apply, so a delivery business that does high mileage may find it costly.
considerations: Seasonal income

If the business is quiet in January or winter, fixed monthly payments continue regardless. Ask whether a seasonal payment plan or a longer term is available, and compare the extra interest against the cash flow benefit.
Whole running cost

Insurance for a commercial vehicle, refrigeration servicing, fuel and low-emission zone charges add to the monthly payment. Work out the true monthly cost before deciding whether the vehicle earns its place.
When it is not the right fit

A business that only occasionally needs a vehicle may do better hiring one or using a courier. Where the vehicle is a small part of a bigger plan, an unsecured loan covering the whole project can be simpler than a separate agreement.
faqs: Can a restaurant get finance for a delivery van?

Yes, if the company is a limited company or LLP that has traded for six months or more. Lenders usually want to see that delivery income or catering work will cover the payments. A broker can explain how to present this, and which lenders are comfortable with hospitality businesses.
Is it better to lease or buy a refrigerated vehicle?

Buying through hire purchase suits a vehicle you will run for many years, while contract hire suits a business that wants to replace it every three or four years. Refrigeration units add maintenance cost, so check whether servicing is included. The tax and VAT treatment also differs, so ask your accountant.
Can I finance an electric van?

Yes. Many lenders finance electric vehicles in the same way as diesel ones, though values and residuals may be assessed differently. Charging at your premises or depot is worth planning for, and some businesses finance the charger alongside the vehicle. A broker can explain how lenders in this market treat electric stock.
Do I need a deposit?

Many agreements ask for a deposit, often between 10% and 20% of the vehicle’s price, though this varies with the lender, the vehicle and the strength of the company’s accounts. A larger deposit can reduce the monthly payment. A broker can tell you what a lender is likely to expect.
What if my business model changes and I no longer need the vehicle?

You normally remain liable for the agreement, because it is a commitment for the full term. Some agreements allow early settlement for a fee, or the vehicle can be sold and the finance repaid. Ask about early repayment terms before signing, as they vary between lenders.

buying-equipment|construction-and-trades.h1: Finance for buying equipment in construction and trades
buying-equipment|construction-and-trades.title: Equipment Finance for Construction and Trades | Loanleaf
buying-equipment|construction-and-trades.desc: How UK builders, contractors and trades finance plant, tools and machinery, and which loan types tend to suit. One short form, a specialist broker.
buying-equipment|construction-and-trades.lead: Plant and specialist tools earn money on site, so the finance works best when payments sit alongside the contracts that use them.
intro: Construction and trades businesses buy equipment that is expensive, hard-wearing and often needed for a specific job: a mini digger, scaffolding, a concrete mixer, a cherry picker, a laser level set or a CNC bender. Buying outright can use up the cash the business needs to pay subcontractors and suppliers, because many contractors wait 30 to 60 days for payment and retentions can hold back 5% for a year or more. Finance spreads that cost across the jobs the kit works on.

Asset finance is the common answer, usually hire purchase for plant the business will keep and a lease or hire agreement for kit used on a single contract. Hire purchase usually leaves you owning the equipment at the end. A broker will want to see the contracts or order book that the equipment supports, because lenders feel more confident when they can see where the income comes from. Most lenders will ask what work the equipment is for.
uses: Plant for a new contract
A groundworks company wins a drainage contract and finances a mini digger and dumper so the work can start without waiting for the first stage payment.
Replacing worn-out tools
An electrical contractor refreshes testers, cable pullers and scaffold towers on a rolling basis, financing the larger items and paying cash for the smaller ones.
Scaffolding and access equipment
A scaffolding firm buys a new batch of tube, boards and fittings, which generally holds its value, and finances it over three to five years to match its working life.
Specialist machinery for a trade
A joinery workshop financing a CNC router or a plumbing firm buying a drain camera and jetting kit, because the machine brings in work it could not take on before.
fit: Typical amounts and terms

Smaller plant such as a compact excavator might be £20,000 to £60,000 over three to five years, while bigger items can reach six figures. Lenders match the term to how long the equipment will last and its likely resale value, so well-known brands of plant usually finance more easily.
What lenders look at

They look at the company’s trading history, whether contracts are in place, bank statements showing the cash cycle, and existing finance commitments. Because construction payment can be uneven, lenders often want to understand retentions, pay-when-paid terms and how late payments are handled.
Fitting payments to the cash cycle

A fixed monthly payment is straightforward, but if the business is paid in stages it may be worth asking about stepped or deferred first payments. Agreements can also be structured with a balloon, which lowers monthly cost but leaves a final sum to pay or refinance.
considerations: Utilisation
Equipment that sits idle between jobs still has to be paid for. Be honest about how many days a month it will work, and consider hire for equipment used only occasionally.
Depreciation and condition

Plant can lose value quickly if it is worked hard, which matters if you plan to sell it before the agreement ends. Keep service records, because they help both resale value and any future finance applications.
When it is not the right fit
If the squeeze comes from late customer payments rather than a purchase, invoice finance or a revolving facility may deal with the cause better. A broker can explain how each works for a contractor.
faqs: Can a start-up contractor finance plant?

Loanleaf is for limited companies and LLPs that have traded for at least six months with annual revenue of £50,000 or more. Newer trading businesses would need to wait. A broker can explain what lenders want to see, such as contract records and bank statements, once the company reaches that point.
Is it better to buy or hire plant for a single job?

Hire is usually simpler for a one-off job because there is no commitment beyond the contract, while financing makes sense when you expect to use the equipment regularly. A rough test is how many days a year it will work. A broker or your accountant can help you run the numbers.
Can I finance used machinery?

Often yes, particularly from dealers or auction houses with clear paperwork. Lenders will consider age, hours and condition, and may ask for a valuation. Terms tend to be shorter than for new equipment, and some lenders will not finance items over a certain age. A broker can say which lenders handle older plant.
Does the equipment count as security?

Usually yes. In asset finance the equipment is the lender’s main security, so a separate property charge is not normally needed. A director’s personal guarantee may still be requested. Check the agreement carefully, and ask the broker to explain exactly what you are signing for.
What if a contract is cancelled and I no longer need the machine?

The finance agreement remains in place, because it is a separate commitment from the contract. You could redeploy the machine, sell it and settle the finance, or negotiate an early settlement. Ask about early repayment charges before you sign, because they differ between lenders.

buying-vehicles|construction-and-trades.h1: Finance for buying vehicles in construction and trades
buying-vehicles|construction-and-trades.title: Vehicle Finance for Construction and Trades | Loanleaf
buying-vehicles|construction-and-trades.desc: How UK builders, electricians, plumbers and contractors finance vans, pickups and tippers, and which loan types tend to suit. Free introduction to a broker.
buying-vehicles|construction-and-trades.lead: Vans, pickups and tippers carry the tools and the work, so the finance has to cope with hard use and fast-growing mileage.
intro: For a trades business the van is the workshop. An electrician carries stock and test equipment, a builder needs a tipper or pickup, and a landscaper may run a tractor unit with a trailer. These vehicles get loaded, mudded and driven every day, so mileage climbs quickly and their value falls with it. As the team grows, each new tradesperson usually needs a vehicle, which can mean £30,000 to £40,000 per hire on top of wages. A broker can help you plan for that.

Hire purchase is the common route for vehicles the business will keep, because there are no mileage limits and the business owns the vehicle at the end. Contract hire suits operators who want predictable costs and regular replacement, though mileage and condition rules apply. A broker will ask how many vehicles you run, how heavily they are used and how the work they carry is paid for. Think about how many vehicles the team really needs.
uses: Adding a van for a new employee
A plumbing firm takes on an apprentice-turned-engineer and finances an extra van so the new hire is productive straight away.
Replacing a high-mileage fleet
A heating contractor swaps three vans that are over 150,000 miles for newer ones, spreading the cost rather than buying them in a single quarter.
Tippers, flatbeds and pickups
A groundworks firm finances a tipper for hauling spoil and materials, a heavier purchase with a longer term and different insurance.
Specialist conversions
A drainage business or locksmith orders a van with racking, jetting kit or a vacuum system fitted, and finances the vehicle and the conversion together.
fit: Typical amounts and terms

A light panel van might be £20,000 to £40,000, a tipper £35,000 to £70,000 and larger commercial vehicles more. Terms are commonly three to five years, shorter for higher-mileage vehicles, with a deposit asked for in many cases.
What lenders look at

They want to see that the business trades profitably, whether any existing vehicle finance is up to date and how many vehicles the company already runs. Because the vehicle is the security, make, age and mileage matter, and popular models usually finance more easily than unusual conversions.
Ownership against flexibility

Hire purchase suits tradespeople who keep vehicles until they wear out, while contract hire often includes servicing at a monthly price but charges for excess mileage and damage. A sensible comparison looks at total cost over the time you realistically keep the vehicle.
considerations: Mileage and wear
Tradespeople’s vans often come back with dents, shelving marks and high mileage. Leases charge for excess mileage and damage beyond fair wear, so be realistic about how hard the van will work.
Commercial insurance and tax
Insurance for tools in transit, fuel, tyres and the cost of vehicle tax add to the monthly payment. For VAT and tax treatment of hire purchase against leasing, ask your accountant.
When it is not the right fit

If a van is needed only for a short contract, short-term rental will probably cost less than a multi-year agreement. If you want to finance vehicles and tools together, a broker may suggest an unsecured loan or a combined asset package.
faqs: Can I finance several vans at once?

Yes. Many lenders will finance several vehicles under one facility or a set of agreements, which can simplify paperwork and budgeting. The lender will look at the company as a whole, including existing vehicle finance. A broker can explain whether a fleet arrangement or separate deals gives a better fit.
What is the difference between hire purchase and contract hire for a van?

With hire purchase you pay instalments and usually own the van after the final payment, with no mileage limit. With contract hire you pay to use the van for a set period and hand it back, subject to mileage and condition terms. Each treats VAT differently, so ask your accountant.
Can I get finance for a used van?

Often yes, particularly from a registered dealer. Lenders consider age, mileage and value, and some set limits such as a maximum age at the end of the agreement. Terms are usually shorter than for new vehicles and the deposit may be larger. A broker can explain what lenders accept.
Do vans lose value quickly?

Commercial vehicles generally depreciate with age and mileage, and a heavily used tradesperson’s van can lose value faster than a lightly used one. This matters if you plan to sell it before the finance ends. Regular servicing and clear records help support resale value.
Will a director need to give a personal guarantee?

Some lenders ask for one, especially for newer or smaller companies or higher-value vehicles, while others will lend on the strength of the business and the vehicle alone. It is worth asking the broker before you apply, and reading what a guarantee would commit you to.

buying-equipment|retail.h1: Finance for buying equipment in retail
buying-equipment|retail.title: Equipment Finance for Retail Businesses | Loanleaf
buying-equipment|retail.desc: How UK independent shops and multi-site retailers finance tills, shop fittings, refrigeration and stockroom equipment, and which loans tend to suit.
buying-equipment|retail.lead: Shop fit-outs and display equipment are paid for before the first sale, so retailers usually spread the cost over the years the fittings last.
intro: Retail equipment is mostly about getting the shop ready to trade and keeping it working. That covers tills and card terminals, shelving and display units, lighting, refrigeration for a food or convenience store, security systems and the racking and conveyors in a stockroom. A new store can need £50,000 or more in fittings before a single sale, and refits every five to seven years keep the shop looking current. Spreading the cost keeps cash free for stock.

Asset finance covers equipment that can be identified and valued, such as refrigeration, tills and stockroom machinery, usually through hire purchase or leasing. Fixtures built into a shop, such as bespoke joinery, may be harder to finance as an asset, in which case an unsecured loan can work. A broker will want to know how many sites you run and how steady your card takings and footfall have been. Both are common in retail.
uses: Fitting out a new unit
Shelving, lighting, a till system, signage and changing rooms are bought together and financed over several years, so the opening budget stays available for stock.
Refrigeration for a food retailer
A convenience store or deli replaces chilled display units that are failing, spreading the cost rather than risking spoiled stock and lost sales.
Modernising the tills and card systems
A multi-site retailer rolls out new point-of-sale software and hardware to link stock and sales across locations, often through leasing so the kit can be upgraded.
Stockroom and click-and-collect equipment
Racking, a labelling machine and a collection lockers system are financed to speed up online orders handled from the shop.
fit: Typical amounts and terms

Individual items such as chiller units or till systems might be £2,000 to £20,000, while a full fit-out can reach £100,000 or more. Terms are commonly two to seven years, with shorter terms for technology that dates quickly and longer for durable fittings.
What lenders look at

They look at how long the shop has traded, the pattern of card takings, rent and lease length, and the profit after paying stock. A short lease can worry a lender because fixtures may have to be removed, so the remaining lease term is often part of the assessment.
Choosing the structure

Hire purchase suits durable items you will keep, such as refrigeration. Leasing suits technology that you expect to replace, because the equipment can be swapped at the end. A broker can also look at whether a business loan covering both equipment and stock would be simpler.
considerations: Lease length and landlord
Shop fittings are only useful for as long as you hold the premises. If a lease is short or about to be renegotiated, committing to a long finance term on fixtures carries risk.
Technology moves quickly
A till system financed over seven years can feel outdated long before the final payment. Match the term to how long the technology will stay useful and consider leasing for software-led hardware.
When it is not the right fit

Stock purchases, seasonal peaks and general cash flow are not equipment needs. For those, a revolving credit facility or merchant cash advance usually suits better than an asset agreement, and a broker can explain the difference.
faqs: Can I finance shop fittings that are fixed to the premises?

It can be harder, because fixed fittings may not be removable and so have little resale value to a lender. Some lenders will still consider them, often with a larger deposit or a shorter term, while others suggest an unsecured loan. A broker can explain which route lenders prefer for a particular fit-out.
Is leasing or hire purchase better for tills and card terminals?

Leasing often suits technology that you expect to replace, because the kit can be upgraded when the term ends. Hire purchase suits equipment you plan to keep. Software subscriptions are usually separate from the hardware agreement. Check how each option is treated for VAT and tax with your accountant.
Does my shop need to have been trading for long?

Loanleaf is for limited companies and LLPs that have traded for at least six months with annual revenue of £50,000 or more. For a new unit, lenders may look at the company’s wider results and ask for a business plan. A broker can explain what they would want to see.
Can I finance equipment for several shops at once?

Yes. Multi-site retailers can sometimes arrange a single facility covering equipment for several locations, which simplifies paperwork. Lenders will look at the whole group’s trading and borrowing. A broker can advise whether one facility or a set of separate agreements suits your plans better.
What if a store closes before the finance ends?

The agreement continues, because it is a commitment of the company. The equipment can sometimes be moved to another shop, sold with the lender’s agreement or returned under a lease. Early settlement may involve charges. Ask about this before you sign, particularly if you may close or relocate stores.

buying-vehicles|retail.h1: Finance for buying vehicles in retail
buying-vehicles|retail.title: Vehicle Finance for Retail Businesses | Loanleaf
buying-vehicles|retail.desc: How UK retailers finance delivery vans, furniture lorries and pick-up vehicles, and which loan types tend to suit. One short form, a specialist broker.
buying-vehicles|retail.lead: Most shops run vehicles only for delivery, and the question is whether delivery earns enough to carry a van for several years.
intro: Plenty of retailers never need a vehicle, but those that deliver do. A furniture or appliance shop with a two-person delivery crew, a garden centre moving bulky stock, a bakery or deli with a local round, or a wholesale-retail hybrid collecting stock from suppliers all depend on one or two vans that are used most days. The vehicle is a cost that has to be paid for out of delivery charges, higher basket values or saved courier fees. That is the case to test first.

Because the vehicle is easily valued, asset finance is the usual route, most often hire purchase. A retailer who delivers every day and wants to own the van may choose hire purchase, while one that wants to replace it every few years may prefer contract hire. A broker will ask how the vehicle contributes to sales, as lenders like to see that the payments are sensible against that work. Work out what delivery earns before choosing a structure.
uses: Delivery vans for a furniture or appliance shop
A larger van with a tail lift and two drivers is financed so customers can be offered delivery on bulky items, which can lift the order value.
A van for a garden centre or builders’ merchant
A flatbed or box van delivers plants, compost and building supplies to local trade customers, replacing expensive third-party hauliers.
A local delivery round
A bakery, butcher or delicatessen finances a small refrigerated van for a regular route to cafés and homes, with the term set against how long the route has run.
Replacing an old vehicle
An ageing van fails its test and costs more in repairs than a financed replacement would in monthly payments.
fit: Typical amounts and terms

A small van might cost £15,000 to £30,000 and a Luton or box van with a tail lift £35,000 to £60,000. Terms are commonly three to five years, with a deposit often asked for, particularly for specialist or higher-value vehicles.
What lenders look at

Lenders look at the retailer’s trading record and whether the vehicle’s cost is sensible compared with the business’s size. They check existing finance and the vehicle’s value, since it is the security. For a retailer, they may ask how deliveries are charged and how often the vehicle is used.
Own, lease or use a courier

Hire purchase gives ownership and no mileage limit. Contract hire may include servicing and fixed monthly costs, but mileage and wear are charged. If the vehicle will do only a few trips a week, a courier or van hire can cost less than any finance agreement.
considerations: Utilisation
A van that sits at the shop three days out of five still costs the same each month. Count your likely delivery days and compare the total cost with the delivery income or courier fees you would save.
Drivers and compliance
Larger vehicles need appropriate licences, insurance and, in some cases, tachographs. Check these before choosing a vehicle size, as a heavier van can add cost and complexity.
When it is not the right fit

If the real constraint is cash for stock, an equipment or vehicle agreement will not solve it. A revolving credit facility or unsecured loan may suit better, and a broker can explain how each would fit a retailer’s seasonal pattern.
faqs: Is it worth financing a van for deliveries?

It can be if deliveries earn money, either through charges or higher sales, and if the monthly payment plus running costs is lower than using a courier. A simple comparison of delivery numbers, fees and costs helps. A broker can explain the finance side, and your accountant can help with the business case.
Can I finance a van with a tail lift or refrigeration?

Yes, many lenders finance specialist vehicles and conversions, though they may lend less against modifications that are hard to resell. Ask for the vehicle and conversion to be financed together if possible. Lenders may ask for a supplier quote and the vehicle’s specification, and a broker can explain what they need.
Do I need a deposit for a van?

Many agreements ask for a deposit, often 10% to 20% of the price, although some lenders will finance a larger share for well-established companies. The deposit lowers the monthly payment. A broker can say what a lender is likely to ask for given your accounts and the vehicle.
Can several shops share a vehicle?

Yes, but the finance is in the company’s name, so the lender will look at the company’s wider trading rather than any individual shop. If the shops are separate companies, they need separate agreements, or a group guarantee. A broker can explain how a group structure affects the application.
What happens at the end of a hire purchase agreement?

After the final payment, and any option-to-purchase fee, ownership of the vehicle passes to the business. You can keep running it, sell it or trade it in. Contract hire works differently: you hand the vehicle back, with any charges for mileage or damage. Read the end-of-term terms carefully before you choose.

buying-equipment|manufacturing.h1: Finance for buying equipment in manufacturing
buying-equipment|manufacturing.title: Equipment Finance for Manufacturing Businesses | Loanleaf
buying-equipment|manufacturing.desc: How UK manufacturers and fabricators finance CNC machines, presses, lines and tooling, and which loan types tend to suit. Free introduction to a broker.
buying-equipment|manufacturing.lead: Production machinery is the largest purchase most manufacturers make, so the finance has to be judged against output, not just price.
intro: Machinery is how a manufacturer makes money, and it is the biggest single outlay in most workshops. A five-axis CNC machine, a laser cutter, an injection moulding press, a packaging line or a paint booth can each cost from £50,000 to well over £500,000. Machines also come with extras such as tooling, installation, software and training, which a finance quote should ideally cover. Spreading the cost over the years a machine produces is how most manufacturers keep cash free for materials and wages, and for the next order.

Asset finance is the established route. Hire purchase suits a machine the factory will keep for ten years, while leasing can suit equipment that needs replacing sooner. Because machinery is easy to value and often resalable, lenders can often arrange it more readily than an unsecured loan of the same size. A broker will look at how the machine improves capacity, scrap rates or margin, because that is the case lenders want to see.
uses: A new CNC or laser cutter
A fabricator buys a machine that can take on work currently outsourced, financing it over five to seven years so payments sit below the margin the extra work earns.
A production line upgrade
A food or packaging manufacturer replaces a line to raise output or meet a customer’s new specification, often as a staged purchase.
Tooling and moulds
A plastics business finances new moulds for a customer contract, with the term matched to the length of that contract rather than the machine’s life.
Refinancing existing machinery
A manufacturer that owns equipment outright raises cash against it through asset refinance, keeping production running while releasing money for a different part of the business.
fit: Typical amounts and terms

Mid-range machines are often £30,000 to £250,000, with large lines and presses higher. Terms commonly run from three to seven years, longer for heavy plant with a long working life, and lenders usually ask for a deposit that varies with the machine and your accounts.
What lenders look at

They look at the company’s accounts, order book and key customers, because a machine that depends on one contract is riskier. They also look at resale value: widely used makes from known suppliers are easier to finance than one-off or highly customised machines.
Installation and staged payments

Large machines are delivered and commissioned over weeks or months. Some lenders support staged drawdown or pre-delivery payments to the supplier, which matters when a manufacturer is paying for a machine that is not yet producing.
considerations: Customisation and resale value
The more a machine is built to a unique specification, the less a lender can get if it has to be sold. Expect lower advances or larger deposits for bespoke equipment.
Downtime and commissioning
A machine that is delayed or slow to reach full output still carries payments. Build a buffer into your plans for installation, training and ramp-up before the new output covers the cost.
When it is not the right fit

If cash is tied up in raw materials or slow-paying customers rather than machinery, invoice finance or a revolving credit facility addresses the cause more directly. A broker can advise how to separate those needs.
faqs: How do lenders value specialist machinery?

They look at the make and model, age, condition and how easily a similar machine can be sold. Common brands with an active used market are easier than one-off builds. Lenders may ask for a supplier invoice, specifications and sometimes an independent valuation. A broker can tell you how lenders view the particular equipment.
Can I finance machinery from an overseas supplier?

Often yes, though it can require extra checks on the supplier, the currency and import costs. Some lenders will pay the supplier directly, and some will include delivery and installation in the amount financed. Bring the quote and shipping terms to the broker early, as the structure can affect timing.
What is asset refinance?

It lets a company that already owns equipment raise cash against it, usually by selling it to a lender and leasing it back, or borrowing against its value. It can release money for other uses, but you pay interest and take on a new commitment. A broker can explain whether it suits your situation.
Is hire purchase or leasing better for factory equipment?

Hire purchase suits machines you will run for years, because you usually own them at the end. Leasing can suit equipment that may be upgraded, with payments treated differently for tax and VAT. The right choice depends on your accounting and plans, so ask your accountant before agreeing.
Can a manufacturer finance software and installation as well?

Sometimes. Many lenders will include delivery, installation and basic software with the machine in a single agreement, provided these are on the supplier’s invoice. Large or separate software licences can be harder to finance. A broker can say which costs a particular lender is willing to include.

buying-vehicles|manufacturing.h1: Finance for buying vehicles in manufacturing
buying-vehicles|manufacturing.title: Vehicle Finance for Manufacturing Businesses | Loanleaf
buying-vehicles|manufacturing.desc: How UK manufacturers finance delivery vehicles, forklift trucks and site vehicles, and which loan types tend to suit. One short form, a specialist broker.
buying-vehicles|manufacturing.lead: For a manufacturer, vehicles move finished goods and stock, and the question is how many the business needs to run on its own.
intro: Manufacturers use vehicles in two ways. On the road, they run delivery vans and lorries to get goods to customers, sometimes on routes tied to a major buyer’s delivery slots. On site, they run forklifts, yard tractors and other powered vehicles that move materials between stores and production. Some manufacturers run their own transport to control delivery times, while others use hauliers and keep only site vehicles. Which mix suits depends on your volumes and customers.

Both are normally financed as assets. Road vehicles suit hire purchase or contract hire, often over three to seven years depending on size. Forklifts and site trucks are commonly leased or financed on hire purchase and often come with a service plan. A broker will look at how heavily the vehicles are used and whether running your own transport costs less than buying it in, because lenders consider the same question.
uses: A delivery lorry for a major customer
A food or components manufacturer finances a 7.5 tonne lorry or rigid so it can meet a retailer’s tight delivery windows, rather than relying on a third party.
Forklifts and reach trucks
A factory replaces ageing trucks with new ones on a lease that includes servicing, which spreads the cost and avoids surprise repair bills.
Vans for installation and service teams
A manufacturer of windows, signs or equipment finances vans for the fitting teams that deliver and install the product at customers’ premises.
Yard and site vehicles
A tug, yard tractor or electric site vehicle is financed to move trailers and loads around the site more efficiently.
fit: Typical amounts and terms

A delivery van might be £20,000 to £40,000, a 7.5 tonne rigid £60,000 to £100,000 and an articulated unit more. Forklifts range from around £15,000 to £60,000 or more, and terms usually run from three to seven years with a deposit.
What lenders look at

They look at the company’s accounts, existing vehicle commitments and how the vehicle is used. For heavier vehicles they may ask about operator licensing and compliance. Forklifts hold value well when they are from a main brand and have service history, which helps both the term and the advance.
Service plans and total cost

Many forklift and vehicle agreements offer servicing and maintenance bundled into the monthly payment, which makes budgeting easier but can raise the overall cost. Compare a bundled price against buying servicing separately, over the realistic time you will use the vehicle.
considerations: Own transport or buy it in

A vehicle also needs a driver, insurance, maintenance and compliance. For lower volumes, a haulier or courier may cost less overall than running your own lorry, so test that before committing to payments.
Compliance for heavier vehicles
Lorries and some vans have operator licence, tachograph and driver hours requirements, and forklifts need trained operators. These add to the real cost and administrative load.
When it is not the right fit

If a manufacturer’s cash is stuck in unpaid invoices, a vehicle will not fix it. Invoice finance or a revolving credit facility may suit better, and a broker can explain how each works alongside an asset agreement.
faqs: Can I finance forklifts and site vehicles?

Yes. Forklifts, tugs and similar vehicles are commonly financed by hire purchase or leased, often with a service package. Lenders consider the make, model and age, so mainstream brands are usually easier. A broker can arrange finance for one or several trucks and explain the difference between buying and leasing for your site.
Is it cheaper to run our own lorry than use hauliers?

It depends on volume, routes and how much control you need. A lorry brings finance payments, a driver, insurance, fuel and compliance costs, and it is only efficient if it is used most days. Compare the total cost with your current haulage spend before deciding, and ask your accountant to check the figures.
Do lenders finance heavy goods vehicles?

Yes, many do, though larger vehicles may require a bigger deposit, and shorter terms for older vehicles. Lenders consider the vehicle’s make, age, mileage and the company’s compliance, including operator licensing where relevant. A broker can say which lenders work with heavier vehicles and what documents they need.
Can I finance electric forklifts or vans?

Yes, many lenders finance electric vehicles in the same way as diesel ones, though they may assess resale value differently, particularly for batteries. Charging infrastructure is worth planning for. A broker can explain how lenders currently treat electric stock and whether a charger can be included.
What happens to the vehicle at the end of the term?

With hire purchase, you own it once the final payment and any option fee is made. With a lease or contract hire, you hand it back, and may owe charges for excess mileage or damage. Some agreements allow extension or replacement. Read the end-of-term conditions closely before signing.

buying-equipment|transport-and-logistics.h1: Finance for buying equipment in transport and logistics
buying-equipment|transport-and-logistics.title: Equipment Finance for Transport and Logistics | Loanleaf
buying-equipment|transport-and-logistics.desc: How UK hauliers, couriers and logistics firms finance trailers, tail lifts, telematics, racking and handling kit, and which loans tend to suit.
buying-equipment|transport-and-logistics.lead: Trailers, tail lifts and warehouse kit are bought around the vehicles, and each has its own working life and resale market.
intro: Equipment in logistics is everything that earns money alongside the tractor unit or van: curtainside and refrigerated trailers, tail lifts, pallet trucks, racking, scanners, telematics and tracking systems, and charging points for electric fleets. A trailer can cost £25,000 to £60,000 and outlasts several tractor units, while a warehouse racking installation can run to six figures and is only useful if the lease on the building lasts. Small items add up quickly across a fleet.

Asset finance is the usual route, mostly through hire purchase or leasing, with the equipment as security. Trailers and handling kit from well-known makers have active resale markets, so they tend to be easier to finance than customised equipment. A broker will ask which contracts the equipment supports, because lenders prefer to see payments covered by named customers rather than by hopeful spot work. That evidence usually shapes the term offered.
uses: Adding trailers for a new contract
A haulier wins a regular route and finances two curtainside trailers, with payments set against the contract’s monthly value.
Tail lifts and refrigeration units
A multi-drop courier adds tail lifts to its vans to handle heavier parcels, or a chilled distributor replaces failing refrigeration units before the summer.
Racking and handling in a warehouse
A fulfilment operator installs racking, a conveyor and scanners to take on a new client, financing them over the term of the client contract.
Telematics and tracking
A fleet fits tracking and driver-behaviour systems to cut fuel use and insurance costs, often as a lease or subscription alongside the vehicles.
fit: Typical amounts and terms

Trailers are typically £20,000 to £70,000, with specialist or refrigerated units higher. Handling equipment ranges widely, and a racking project can be six figures. Terms are often three to seven years, longer for trailers with a long working life, and a deposit is common.
What lenders look at

They look at the company’s trading record, the contracts supporting the equipment and the age and make of the asset. Operator licensing and a history of keeping vehicles compliant matter for road haulage. A fleet with clean maintenance records and a mix of customers is easier to finance than one dependent on a single buyer.
Matching the term to the contract

If equipment is bought for a specific contract, lenders and brokers will often look at how long the contract runs. A seven-year trailer agreement on a one-year contract is a bigger risk, so the term and any break clause should line up with how you expect to use the equipment.
considerations: Single-customer risk

If one customer provides most of the income that supports the equipment, losing that contract can leave payments with no work behind them. Think about whether you could redeploy the equipment elsewhere.
Fuel, rates and compliance
Equipment is only one part of operating cost. Insurance, driver wages, fuel, tolls and compliance work all compete for the same revenue, so build the full cost before agreeing a new commitment.
When it is not the right fit

If the squeeze comes from waiting 60 days for customers to pay, equipment finance will add another payment rather than fix the gap. Invoice finance or a revolving facility may deal with that more directly.
faqs: Can I finance a trailer separately from a tractor unit?

Yes. Trailers are usually financed as separate assets, often with a longer term than the tractor unit because they last longer. Lenders will consider the type, age and make. A broker can arrange separate agreements or a combined facility, depending on which gives you better flexibility.
Is leasing or hire purchase better for logistics equipment?

Hire purchase suits long-lived equipment such as trailers and racking because you usually own it at the end. Leasing may suit technology such as scanners and telematics, which is replaced more often. Tax and VAT treatment differs between them, so ask your accountant which fits your accounts.
Can I get finance for charging points for an electric fleet?

Sometimes. Chargers can be financed as equipment, either alone or alongside the vehicles, and some lenders offer specific schemes. Installation costs and grid connection can be harder to include. A broker can say what a lender may fund, and whether grants or other schemes are worth checking separately.
Does my contract need to be long enough to cover the finance?

It is not a strict rule, but lenders and brokers often like to see that income covers payments with some margin, and a short contract for long-term equipment can concern them. A multi-customer business is more comfortable than a single-contract one. A broker can talk through the structure with you.
Can I finance used trailers or handling equipment?

Often yes, particularly from dealers with clear paperwork. Lenders look at age, condition and the used market for the make, and may ask for a valuation or inspection. Terms are usually shorter and deposits may be larger. A broker can advise which lenders handle older equipment.

buying-vehicles|transport-and-logistics.h1: Finance for buying vehicles in transport and logistics
buying-vehicles|transport-and-logistics.title: Vehicle Finance for Transport and Logistics | Loanleaf
buying-vehicles|transport-and-logistics.desc: How UK hauliers, couriers and logistics firms finance vans, rigids and tractor units, and which loan types tend to suit. Free introduction to a broker.
buying-vehicles|transport-and-logistics.lead: For a haulier or courier the vehicle is the business, so finance is judged on utilisation, contracts and residual value.
intro: Transport firms are the most vehicle-dependent businesses there are, and fleet decisions are made against utilisation: a van that runs 250 days a year is a different proposition from one that runs 150. A tractor unit can cost £70,000 to £110,000 and a rigid lorry or large van £40,000 to £90,000. A growing firm may add one or two vehicles at a time, usually when a contract or route is confirmed.

Hire purchase is the common route for vehicles that will be run to the end of their life, while contract hire and leasing can suit fleets that replace vehicles on a regular cycle and want maintenance bundled in. Lenders know the sector and its resale markets well, so vehicle age, mileage and spec are all checked. A broker will look at your contracts, fleet age, compliance record and how many vehicles you already finance.
uses: Adding a vehicle for a new route
A courier takes on a delivery round for an online retailer and finances a van to serve it, with payments set against the contract.
Replacing an ageing tractor unit
A haulier replaces a unit with high mileage and rising repair bills, moving to a newer vehicle that is more efficient and less likely to fail on the road.
Moving to electric or low-emission vehicles
A last-mile operator switches part of its fleet to electric vans to meet city access rules, financing them alongside chargers at the depot.
Refinancing the fleet
A firm that owns vehicles outright borrows against them to release cash for a new depot or extra drivers, or consolidates several existing agreements.
fit: Typical amounts and terms

Vans are commonly £20,000 to £50,000, rigids £50,000 to £100,000 and tractor units £70,000 to £120,000. Terms generally run three to seven years depending on the vehicle and its expected mileage, with deposits common and sometimes balloons to lower monthly payments.
What lenders look at

They look at the company’s trading record, contracts or customer spread, existing finance, and operator licence and compliance history for heavier vehicles. The vehicle’s spec, age and mileage matter, since it is the security. A fleet with a record of keeping up payments is easier to finance than a first-time borrower.
Ownership against flexibility

Hire purchase gives ownership and no mileage limit, so it suits a firm running vehicles hard. Contract hire provides predictable monthly costs and often includes maintenance, but mileage and damage charges apply, so high-mileage operators should check the limits carefully.
considerations: Utilisation and downtime
A vehicle that is parked costs the same as one on the road. Set payments against realistic working days, and plan for breakdowns, MOT time and driver absence.
Concentration and contract loss
If one customer accounts for most of a vehicle’s work, losing that contract can strand the payments. A broker may suggest keeping term and break options flexible.
When it is not the right fit

If cash is short because customers pay late rather than because vehicles are old, invoice finance or a revolving facility may deal with it better. A broker can explain how it would sit alongside your vehicle agreements.
faqs: Can I finance a vehicle with a balloon payment?

Many lenders offer agreements where a final lump sum is due at the end, which lowers monthly payments. You then pay it, refinance it or sell the vehicle to settle it. The risk is that the vehicle may be worth less than the balloon. A broker can explain the figures and how this affects your cash flow.
Do lenders finance older HGVs?

Some do, subject to age and mileage limits, usually with shorter terms and bigger deposits. Lenders look at how old the vehicle will be at the end of the agreement as well as when it starts. A broker can say which lenders handle older vehicles and what condition or inspection evidence they ask for.
Does my operator licence matter for finance?

For vehicles over a certain weight, lenders typically want to see a valid operator licence and a clean compliance record, because that affects whether the business can trade. They may ask for details of your transport manager and any enforcement history. A broker can tell you what a lender is likely to ask.
How does a fleet facility differ from separate agreements?

A fleet facility covers multiple vehicles under one arrangement, which can simplify paperwork and make adding vehicles quicker. Separate agreements keep each vehicle independent, which can help if you want to sell or return some. A broker can explain which suits the size and pattern of your fleet.
Can I get finance for electric vans and chargers?

Yes. Many lenders finance electric vehicles in the same way as diesel ones, though valuations of batteries and residuals are assessed carefully. Chargers can sometimes be included or financed separately, depending on installation. A broker can explain how lenders view electric fleets and what documents they will request.

buying-equipment|healthcare-and-dental.h1: Finance for buying equipment in healthcare and dental
buying-equipment|healthcare-and-dental.title: Equipment Finance for Healthcare and Dental | Loanleaf
buying-equipment|healthcare-and-dental.desc: How UK dental practices, clinics and care providers finance chairs, scanners, imaging and treatment equipment, and which loan types tend to suit.
buying-equipment|healthcare-and-dental.lead: Clinical equipment is expensive, regulated and quickly outdated, so healthcare providers tend to match the term to how long it will stay useful.
intro: A dental surgery can cost £50,000 to £100,000 to equip per room, with a chair, delivery unit, light, X-ray, intraoral scanner and sterilisation. Clinics buy ultrasound, laser, physiotherapy or diagnostic equipment, and care homes buy beds, hoists and nurse call systems. Much of it must meet regulatory standards, be serviced regularly and be replaced as technology improves, so the right term is usually shorter than the physical life of the machine. Spreading the cost lets a practice add capacity before the income arrives.

Asset finance is the most common route, with hire purchase for equipment you will keep and leasing for technology that is likely to be replaced. Lenders are generally comfortable with healthcare because revenue is steady and equipment has a resale market. A broker will ask about your patient base, NHS and private mix, and how the equipment will support income, such as new treatments or reduced outsourcing. Clinical equipment is usually the largest cost after staff.
uses: Equipping a new surgery or treatment room
A dental practice adds a surgery with a chair, X-ray and instruments, financing the whole package so the room opens before the practice has built up its new patient list.
Digital dentistry and imaging
A practice buys a CBCT scanner and an intraoral scanner to offer implants and same-day crowns, spreading the cost across the extra treatments it will provide.
Replacing ageing clinical equipment
A physiotherapy or aesthetics clinic replaces lasers or treatment tables that are slow, unreliable or no longer supported by their manufacturer.
Care home equipment
A care provider finances profiling beds, hoists and a new nurse call system, planning payments around fee income per resident.
fit: Typical amounts and terms

A single dental chair package may be £20,000 to £50,000, while imaging equipment can be £30,000 to £120,000 and a fully equipped new surgery higher. Terms are commonly three to seven years, with shorter terms for digital technology and longer for chairs and fixtures.
What lenders look at

They look at the practice’s accounts, the split between NHS and private income, the length of contracts and the number of patients. For a new surgery, they want to see how it will be used. Equipment from established manufacturers with servicing arrangements is easier to finance.
Structure and service

Some agreements bundle servicing or software licences into the payment, which suits equipment that needs regular calibration. Leasing can allow upgrades at the end of the term, which matters for imaging and software that moves fast, though you do not own the equipment.
considerations: Technology moves on

Imaging and scanning equipment can become outdated in a few years. A long finance term on technology that a competitor soon outclasses is a real risk, so match the term to how long the kit will stay useful.
Regulation and servicing
Clinical equipment may need calibration, servicing or registration with regulators. These costs sit on top of the monthly payment, so allow for them.
When it is not the right fit

If you are buying a practice, a commercial mortgage or secured loan may be better than equipment finance alone. Where equipment is a small part of a larger project, an unsecured or secured loan covering the whole project can be simpler.
faqs: Can I finance equipment for a new dental practice?

Possibly, if the company has traded for at least six months and meets Loanleaf’s criteria. A new practice can be harder to finance because there is less trading history, so lenders may look at the clinicians’ experience, a business plan and a deposit. A broker can advise how to present these to lenders.
Is leasing or hire purchase better for dental equipment?

Hire purchase suits items you expect to use for a long time, such as chairs, and gives ownership at the end. Leasing suits digital equipment that will probably need replacing. Tax and VAT treatment differs, and healthcare VAT exemptions can affect the answer, so check with your accountant.
Can I finance a practice refit?

Often equipment such as chairs and imaging can be financed as assets, while building works and fixed fittings are harder because they are not removable. A broker may suggest an unsecured loan or secured loan for the building works and asset finance for the equipment, depending on the lease and the project.
Do lenders treat NHS income differently?

Many lenders see NHS contract income as steady, which helps, but they also look at how long the contract runs and how much of income depends on it. A practice with a mix of NHS and private income is often viewed more favourably than one that is heavily weighted to either. A broker can explain how lenders see your mix.
Can I finance second-hand clinical equipment?

Sometimes, if it comes from a reputable dealer with a service history and clear paperwork. Lenders may be cautious with older digital equipment because its value falls quickly and servicing support can end. Expect a shorter term and a deposit. A broker can explain what lenders will accept.

buying-vehicles|healthcare-and-dental.h1: Finance for buying vehicles in healthcare and dental
buying-vehicles|healthcare-and-dental.title: Vehicle Finance for Healthcare and Dental | Loanleaf
buying-vehicles|healthcare-and-dental.desc: How UK care providers, domiciliary services and clinics finance mobile units, minibuses, adapted vehicles and staff cars, and which loans tend to suit.
buying-vehicles|healthcare-and-dental.lead: Care and clinic vehicles do specific jobs, such as home visits or resident transport, so they are financed around how those services are paid.
intro: Most dental practices do not need vehicles, but other healthcare businesses do. A domiciliary care company needs reliable cars for carers moving between visits, a care home may run an adapted minibus for resident outings and appointments, a mobile dental or optician service operates from a converted van, and a patient transport provider depends on vehicles with ramps or stretchers. Reliability matters because a missed visit affects a vulnerable person.

Asset finance is the standard route. Hire purchase suits adapted vehicles you will keep, while contract hire or leasing suits staff cars replaced regularly and suits a care firm that wants servicing included. Conversions such as wheelchair lifts or medical fit-outs add cost and are harder to resell, so lenders look at them closely. A broker will ask about your contracts, such as local authority or NHS commissions, and how many vehicles you already run.
uses: Cars for a domiciliary care team
A homecare provider finances several small cars for care workers on rounds, replacing mileage claims with company vehicles to improve reliability and cost control.
An adapted minibus
A care home or day centre buys a minibus with a wheelchair lift, financed over a longer term because it is used less heavily than a delivery van.
A mobile clinic or screening unit
A mobile health service finances a converted van with treatment equipment fitted, usually in two parts, the vehicle and the conversion.
Patient transport vehicles
A non-emergency transport firm finances ambulances or wheelchair-accessible vehicles for a contract with a trust or local authority.
fit: Typical amounts and terms

Small cars may be £12,000 to £25,000, an adapted minibus £40,000 to £90,000, and a converted mobile unit more. Terms commonly run three to seven years, with deposits typical for specialist vehicles and shorter terms for high-mileage cars.
What lenders look at

They look at the company’s accounts and how steady its contract income is, such as local authority or NHS contracts, and how long those contracts run. A lender also considers whether the conversion adds resale value or limits it. A broker can often present a contract to show that payments are covered.
Own, lease or contract hire

Hire purchase suits vehicles used for many years, such as an adapted minibus. Contract hire suits staff cars that are replaced every three or four years and can include servicing, which helps predictability. Contract mileage limits matter for domiciliary care teams who cover large rural rounds.
considerations: Contract-dependent income
If a vehicle is financed for a commissioned service and the contract is retendered, the finance may continue after the work stops. Think about whether the vehicle could be redeployed.
Conversions and resale

Wheelchair lifts, medical fit-outs and special livery lower the pool of buyers, so lenders may lend less against them. Compare asking for the base vehicle and the conversion to be financed together or separately.
When it is not the right fit

If staff are paid mileage and the fleet would be small, an allowance or a lease through a payroll scheme could be simpler. For larger needs, a broker may suggest combining vehicle finance with a loan covering the rest of a project.
faqs: Can a care company finance cars for its carers?

Yes, if the company is a limited company or LLP that meets Loanleaf’s criteria. Lenders will look at the contract income and the number of staff on rounds. Some firms prefer contract hire so servicing and replacement are built in. A broker can explain which structure suits your business and the carers’ mileage.
Can I finance a minibus with a wheelchair lift?

Yes, many lenders finance adapted vehicles, though the adaptation may be treated as a separate cost with limited resale value, so a deposit may be larger. The lender may want a quote showing the vehicle and conversion costs. A broker can explain how lenders in this area behave.
How do lenders treat local authority and NHS contracts?

They often see public contracts as steady income, which can support an application, but they also check how long each contract runs and whether it is up for retender. Having contract documents ready helps. A broker can advise how to show the link between the vehicle and the income it supports.
Is contract hire better than hire purchase for staff cars?

It can be if you want predictable monthly costs and replacement every few years, with servicing included. Hire purchase gives ownership and no mileage limit, which suits vehicles you plan to keep. Tax and VAT treatment differs, so ask your accountant before deciding.
Can I finance an ambulance or patient transport vehicle?

Often yes, although vehicles with specialist medical conversions are treated carefully because of limited resale. Lenders may ask for the supplier’s specification, contract evidence and a deposit. A broker can say which lenders work with patient transport and what information speeds up the process.

buying-equipment|ecommerce.h1: Finance for buying equipment in ecommerce
buying-equipment|ecommerce.title: Equipment Finance for Ecommerce Businesses | Loanleaf
buying-equipment|ecommerce.desc: How UK online retailers finance packing lines, warehouse racking, label printers, photography kit and production equipment, and which loans tend to suit.
buying-equipment|ecommerce.lead: An online brand’s equipment is mostly about getting orders out faster, so the sums are smaller and the case is easy to measure.
intro: Ecommerce businesses buy less heavy equipment than manufacturers, but what they buy is tied closely to order volume. As orders grow, packing by hand stops working, so the business buys a label printer, a packing bench, a bag sealer, racking and a conveyor, or fits out a unit of its own. Brands that make their own products may need production equipment, and a photography studio and printing kit can justify themselves by cutting agency costs. Each purchase tends to have a clear payback in time saved.

Asset finance covers equipment that can be identified and valued, such as racking, automation and printers, usually through hire purchase or leasing. Software, photography props and consumables are harder to finance as assets, so an unsecured loan or revolving credit facility may fit better. A broker will look at your sales history, platform data and refund rates, because lenders want to see steady online revenue behind the purchase. Most of this kit is bought as order numbers climb.
uses: Moving from hand packing to a packing line
A brand shipping 300 orders a day finances a conveyor, label printer and packing stations, cutting the time per parcel and the number of temporary staff needed.
Warehouse racking and shelving
A seller moves into a larger unit and finances racking to hold more lines, with the term set to the length of the warehouse lease.
Production or print equipment
A brand that prints or makes its own goods, such as apparel, candles or stationery, finances a heat press, embroidery machine or small production line.
Photography and content studio
A fashion or homeware brand finances camera, lighting and set equipment so product images can be produced in-house.
fit: Typical amounts and terms

Most ecommerce equipment purchases run from £3,000 to £60,000, with automation or production lines higher. Terms are commonly two to five years, longer for racking and shorter for printers and computers, and a deposit is often requested for newer or smaller companies.
What lenders look at

They check trading history, revenue trends, bank statements and how sales are spread across channels. Heavy reliance on one marketplace or advertising source can concern lenders, so evidence of repeat customers and steady margins helps. Lenders also consider whether the equipment is standard and resalable.
Mixing equipment with wider cash needs

Many online brands need stock and advertising money as well as equipment. An unsecured loan or revolving facility can cover the whole plan in one go, while asset finance is cleaner if the equipment is a distinct purchase. A broker can advise on the combination.
considerations: Peak-season risk
Many online businesses make much of their income in a few months. Fixed monthly payments continue through the quiet period, so check you can meet them on a normal month’s sales.
Platform dependence
If most orders come from one marketplace and its rules or fees change, income can drop while payments continue. Lenders may ask about this, and you should too.
When it is not the right fit

If the cash need is for stock before peak or advertising spend, equipment finance does not address it. A revolving credit facility, merchant cash advance or unsecured loan usually fits better, and a broker can explain which works for an online model.
faqs: Can an online-only business get equipment finance?

Yes, if the company is a UK limited company or LLP that has traded for at least six months with annual revenue of £50,000 or more. Lenders will look at online sales history and bank statements rather than a shopfront. A broker can explain how to present platform data and what evidence helps.
Is leasing worthwhile for a label printer or packing equipment?

It can be, particularly for items that may be replaced as volumes grow, and some leases include maintenance. Hire purchase suits equipment you expect to keep. The cost, VAT and tax treatment differ, so compare the full costs over the period you expect to use the item and ask your accountant.
Can I finance racking and shelving for a rented warehouse?

Often yes, but lenders look at the lease length because the racking may need to be removed. A lease with several years left is more comfortable than one near expiry. A broker can advise whether asset finance or an unsecured loan suits the racking plan best.
Can I include software and installation in the agreement?

Sometimes. Installation and delivery on the supplier’s invoice can often be included, but software licences and subscriptions are harder to finance as assets. Some lenders will include basic software that runs the equipment. A broker can say which costs a specific lender will accept in an agreement.
Should I use a loan or asset finance for equipment?

Asset finance is usually simpler for a clear equipment purchase, because the item is security and the payments are matched to its life. An unsecured loan gives more freedom to cover mixed costs but may cost more and be limited in size. A broker can compare the two against your plans.

buying-vehicles|ecommerce.h1: Finance for buying vehicles in ecommerce
buying-vehicles|ecommerce.title: Vehicle Finance for Ecommerce Businesses | Loanleaf
buying-vehicles|ecommerce.desc: How UK online retailers finance delivery vans, cargo bikes and collection vehicles for local delivery and fulfilment, and which loan types tend to suit.
buying-vehicles|ecommerce.lead: Most online sellers use couriers, so a van only makes sense when local delivery, bulky goods or collections justify the payments.
intro: Ecommerce businesses usually post parcels through couriers, so vehicles are not the default purchase. They make sense in particular cases: a furniture or appliance seller delivering bulky items, a food or flower brand with a local same-day offer, a brand that collects stock from suppliers and trade fairs, or a seller running its own network in a few cities. The question is whether the van saves more in courier fees and wins more in sales than it costs. Test that sum before you apply for any finance.

Where a vehicle makes sense, asset finance is the usual route, mostly hire purchase for a van the business will keep and contract hire or leasing where regular replacement or electric vehicles suit. A broker will ask about order volumes, delivery areas and what you currently pay couriers, because lenders want to see a sensible link between the vehicle and the business’s revenue. Many online sellers find couriers cheaper until volumes rise, so check that first, and then look at the finance.
uses: Delivering bulky items directly
A furniture or home brand buys a Luton van with a tail lift to offer white-glove delivery, which supports higher-value orders that couriers handle badly.
Local same-day delivery
A food, drinks or flowers brand finances small vans or electric bikes for a defined area, charging for same-day delivery and keeping control of the customer experience.
Supplier collections and markets
A brand that sells stock at fairs and pop-ups finances a van to carry stands and stock, rather than hiring one for every event.
Returns and fulfilment runs
A seller with a unit across town finances a van to move stock between its warehouse and workshop, or to collect returns from a drop-off point.
fit: Typical amounts and terms

Small vans are commonly £15,000 to £30,000 and larger box or Luton vans £30,000 to £60,000. Electric cargo bikes and smaller vehicles can be lower. Terms generally run three to five years, with deposits common for companies with less trading history.
What lenders look at

They want to see steady online sales, healthy bank statements and no heavy dependence on one platform. The vehicle is the security, so make, age and value matter. For a business buying its first vehicle, lenders may ask how the vehicle will be used and what it will save or earn.
Own, lease or keep using couriers

Hire purchase gives ownership and no mileage limit. Contract hire can include servicing and give predictable costs, which suits low-emission zones and electric vans. If deliveries are only a few a week, a courier or hired van may cost less than any finance agreement.
considerations: Utilisation
A van that is used twice a week costs the same as one that is used six days a week. Count likely delivery days and compare total cost with courier fees before committing.
Running costs and rules
Insurance, fuel or charging, parking, clean air zone charges and driver costs can add significantly to the finance payment. Work these into the plan.
When it is not the right fit

For a business whose challenge is stock or advertising spend, a vehicle will not help. A revolving credit facility, merchant cash advance or unsecured loan may be better, and a broker can explain how each suits online sales patterns.
faqs: Is a van worth it for an online business?

It can be if you deliver bulky or high-value goods, offer local same-day delivery or do frequent collections, and the saving or extra sales outweigh the payments plus running costs. For standard parcels, couriers are usually cheaper. A simple comparison with your current courier spend is a good start.
Can I finance electric cargo bikes or e-vans?

Often yes. Many lenders finance electric vehicles and bikes in the same way as other vehicles, though they treat batteries and residual values carefully. Cargo bikes can be financed as equipment. A broker can explain what lenders accept, and whether charging equipment can be included.
Will lenders worry about my reliance on one marketplace?

They may. Heavy dependence on one marketplace or ad source can make revenue less predictable, so lenders often ask for sales by channel and repeat customer data. A mix of channels, your own site and repeat orders helps. A broker can advise how to show this.
Do I need a driver with specific licences?

It depends on the vehicle. Most vans up to 3.5 tonnes need a standard licence, while heavier vehicles need extra categories and may bring tachograph and operator licensing rules. Check this before choosing, as it affects who can drive and the cost of running the vehicle.
Can a business less than a year old get vehicle finance?

Loanleaf is for limited companies and LLPs that have traded for at least six months with annual revenue of £50,000 or more. Newer companies may be asked for a larger deposit or extra evidence of sales. A broker can explain what lenders usually want to see for a younger online business.

buying-equipment|professional-services.h1: Finance for buying equipment in professional services
buying-equipment|professional-services.title: Equipment Finance for Professional Services | Loanleaf
buying-equipment|professional-services.desc: How UK accountants, architects, consultancies and agencies finance IT, specialist kit and office fit-outs, and which loan types tend to suit.
buying-equipment|professional-services.lead: Professional firms spend on IT, fit-outs and specialist kit rather than heavy machinery, so equipment finance often sits beside a general loan.
intro: A professional services business has few physical assets. It buys laptops, servers, screens and phone systems, then fits out an office. Some firms buy specialist kit, such as survey equipment for a surveyor, printers and plotters for an architect, studio and editing equipment for a creative agency, or secure systems for a law firm. Technology dates fast, and a team of 20 can need £30,000 to £50,000 of kit and fit-out when it moves premises.

Asset finance covers equipment that has a clear resale value, mostly through leasing or hire purchase, with leasing common for IT because kit is refreshed every three to four years. Fit-out works and software are harder to finance as assets, so an unsecured loan is often used instead. A broker will look at your fee income, clients and how steady billing has been, since a professional firm’s main asset is its client base.
uses: Refreshing IT for the team
A consultancy replaces laptops, monitors and network equipment on a leased cycle, keeping costs predictable and the kit current.
Fitting out a new office
An architecture or accountancy practice moves to larger premises and finances furniture and equipment, usually alongside a loan for the fit-out work.
Specialist equipment
A survey practice finances drones, scanners or total stations, or a creative agency finances editing suites and camera kit that bring work in-house.
Secure and compliant systems
A firm handling sensitive data finances a new server, backup system and secure access equipment to meet client or regulatory requirements.
fit: Typical amounts and terms

Most purchases fall between £5,000 and £80,000, with terms of two to five years for IT and longer for furniture or specialist equipment. A deposit is not always needed, particularly for leased IT from established lenders.
What lenders look at

They look at fee income, client concentration, bank statements and how long the firm has traded, since there is little physical security beyond the equipment itself. A firm with several clients and steady billing is generally easier to finance than one dependent on one contract.
Lease or loan
