Leasing suits technology that you will replace, and keeps the refresh cycle simple. An unsecured loan suits mixed spending, such as equipment, fit-out and moving costs together. A broker can compare the structures and explain which costs each can include.
considerations: Rapid depreciation
Laptops and screens fall in value quickly, and a lender may value them lowly. Keep terms short for IT and avoid paying for kit long after it has stopped being useful.
Software and subscriptions
Many professional firms spend more on software than on hardware, and software is harder to finance as an asset. A monthly subscription is an operating cost, not a finance agreement.
When it is not the right fit

If the real need is cash while clients pay slowly, equipment finance does not address it. Invoice finance or a revolving facility may be better, and a broker can suggest the right fit for a fee-earning business.
faqs: Can a services firm finance laptops and IT equipment?

Yes. IT is commonly financed through leasing or hire purchase, and many firms prefer leasing because the equipment is replaced every few years. Lenders will look at the firm’s trading and bank statements. A broker can explain the options and how the cost compares with buying outright.
Is it better to lease or buy IT equipment?

Leasing keeps monthly costs predictable and makes it easier to refresh equipment, while buying outright or on hire purchase gives ownership. The accounting, VAT and tax treatments differ, so your accountant’s view matters. A broker can set out what each lender would offer for the kit you want.
Can I finance an office fit-out?

Parts of it, such as furniture and some equipment, can be financed as assets. Building works and fixed fittings are harder, so many firms use an unsecured loan for the whole project. The lease terms matter because lenders consider how long you will be in the premises. A broker can advise on the structure.
Does a professional firm need to give security?

Asset finance is usually secured on the equipment itself, so extra security is not always needed. Some lenders ask for a personal guarantee from directors, especially for smaller or newer firms. It is worth asking the broker what is likely to be requested and reading the guarantee carefully.
Can I finance specialist equipment such as drones or survey kit?

Often yes, if it comes from a recognised supplier and has a resale market. Lenders will look at value, age and whether the equipment is easy to identify. Highly customised kit can be harder to finance. A broker can say which lenders work with specialist professional equipment.

buying-vehicles|professional-services.h1: Finance for buying vehicles in professional services
buying-vehicles|professional-services.title: Vehicle Finance for Professional Services | Loanleaf
buying-vehicles|professional-services.desc: How UK consultancies, surveyors and agencies finance company cars, site vehicles and shared pool vehicles, and which loan types tend to suit.
buying-vehicles|professional-services.lead: Professional firms rarely need a fleet, so vehicle finance usually means a handful of site or client-visit cars where leasing often beats ownership.
intro: Most professional services firms do not run fleets. Where they need vehicles, the cases are specific: a surveying or engineering practice sends staff to sites in vans or estate cars, a mobile accountancy or inspection business visits clients, and a firm may offer cars to senior staff as part of a package. Because the vehicles are a small part of costs, the focus is on predictable monthly payments and keeping the process simple.

Contract hire and leasing are common, particularly for company cars, because servicing can be included and the car is replaced every three or four years. Hire purchase suits a van or utility vehicle that will be kept for years. Tax treatment of cars is complex, especially for electric vehicles and benefit-in-kind charges for drivers. A broker will ask how many vehicles you need and how they are used, then suggest a structure.
uses: Site vehicles for surveyors and engineers
A surveying practice finances two vans or pickups that carry equipment and staff to site visits, with payments built into project costs.
Cars for client visits
A consultancy leases several cars so staff can travel to clients across the region, with servicing and breakdown cover in a single monthly payment.
Company cars as part of a package
A firm offers electric company cars to senior staff, which can cut benefit-in-kind costs compared with petrol cars, and finances them on contract hire.
A shared pool vehicle
A small firm finances one vehicle for use by several staff for site visits, deliveries of materials and events, rather than reimbursing mileage.
fit: Typical amounts and terms

Cars are usually £20,000 to £50,000 each, vans or pickups £20,000 to £40,000. Terms commonly run two to four years for contract hire and three to five for hire purchase, with deposits varying by lender and by the strength of the firm.
What lenders look at

They look at fee income, the age and trading record of the firm and existing commitments. The vehicle is the security, so make and value matter. For several cars, they may consider a fleet arrangement. Small professional firms with steady billing are generally comfortable lending customers.
Contract hire against ownership

Contract hire is simple and predictable, with mileage and condition limits. Hire purchase gives ownership and flexibility on mileage. For electric vehicles, check the impact on tax for drivers and the firm, because it can change the comparison and your accountant will know the current rules.
considerations: Tax treatment

Company car tax, VAT recovery and capital allowances vary between cars and vans and between structures. Get your accountant’s view before choosing, because the cheapest monthly payment is not always the cheapest overall.
Low usage
A car used for a few client visits a month costs far more per mile than occasional hire or a mileage claim. Look at your real usage before taking on a three-year commitment.
When it is not the right fit

If the need is occasional, rental or paying mileage may be better. If vehicles are a small part of a bigger plan, such as a move or expansion, an unsecured loan covering the whole project can be simpler, and a broker can compare them.
faqs: Is leasing or buying better for company cars?

Leasing, usually through contract hire, is common because payments are predictable, servicing can be included and cars are replaced regularly. Buying on hire purchase gives ownership but exposes you to resale value. Tax treatment, including benefit-in-kind for drivers, differs, so your accountant should look at the figures with you.
Can a small consultancy get vehicle finance?

Yes, if the company is a limited company or LLP that meets Loanleaf’s criteria. Lenders will look at fee income, trading history and bank statements. For a small firm, one or two vehicles is a normal request. A broker can explain how lenders see small professional practices.
Are electric company cars worth considering?

They can be, because benefit-in-kind tax for drivers is generally lower on electric vehicles, and running costs may be lower. Charging, purchase price and range matter, and rules change over time. Your accountant can check the current treatment, and a broker can explain how lenders view electric cars.
Do I need a deposit for contract hire?

Contract hire often asks for an initial rental, commonly a few months’ payments, rather than a deposit in the usual sense. Hire purchase may need a deposit of 10% or more. Requirements vary by lender and company, and a broker can tell you what is likely to be asked.
What if staff leave and I no longer need the car?

The agreement stays with the company, so you would need to reassign the car, settle the agreement early or run to term. Early termination charges can be significant for contract hire. Ask about the terms before signing, particularly if staff numbers may change.
